questions.question: Which mathematical statement formally represents the Archimedean Property for positive real numbers $a$ and $b$?

answerOptions.text: There exists a real number $x$ such that $x a = b$.
answerOptions.rationale: While true in the field of real numbers, this is a property of division and field completeness rather than the Archimedean Property specifically.

answerOptions.text: There exists a positive integer $n$ such that $na > b$.
answerOptions.rationale: This property asserts that no matter how small a positive value $a$ is, adding it to itself enough times will eventually exceed any finite value $b$.

answerOptions.text: For any $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $n(a-b) > 1$.
answerOptions.rationale: This statement is only true under specific conditions where $a > b$, and it is a consequence used in proofs rather than the definition of the property itself.

answerOptions.text: For every positive integer $n$, $na < b$.
answerOptions.rationale: This would imply that $b$ is an infinite bound relative to $a$, which contradicts the Archimedean principle that numbers are finite and comparable.
